title: Optic flow based perception of two-dimensional trajectories and the effects of a single landmark.
research_question: Can human subjects integrate instantaneous perceptions of heading over time to reconstruct a 2D trajectory simulated by optic flow, and how does a single landmark affect this perception and reconstruction?

participants.description: 8 men and 8 women, middle 20s to early 60s, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, naive to experiment purpose. An additional 16 subjects (6 female, 10 male, 8 of whom participated in experiments 1,2,3) participated in a control experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Optic flow stimuli simulating 2D manoeuvres (linear or curvilinear trajectories) over a horizontal ground plane. Environment consisted of 4800 white dots (4 pixel diameter) on a 50x50m ground surface 1m below eye-level, horizon at 15m. Manoeuvres had 3 degrees of freedom: linear/semicircular trajectories, with simulated whole-body orientation fixed in space, fixed relative to path, or changing relative to both. Stimuli included yaw (Ψo) and path rotation (Ψp). Triangular velocity profiles (0 to peak at 4s).

Single landmark: a red dot attached to the ground surface via a string of equally spaced blue dots. Landmarks were either 'shifting' (moved through observer's field of view, fixed in 3D space) or 'fixated' (red dot stationary in middle of screen, simulated movement in depth relative to landmark, eye-level, horizontal eye movements).

measures.instrument: Model vehicle guided on a graphics tablet, recording position (X,Y) and orientation (Φo). Overhead view feedback in HMD.
Calculated from reproduced orientation (Φo) over time.
Calculated as average difference between Φo and Φp.
Count of reproduced manoeuvres classified as rotation in place.

measures.construct: Figural distance (difference between stimulus and response)
measures.instrument: Combined spatial (Dfs) and angular (Dfa) figural distance (Df = √(Dfs²+Dfa²)).

findings.antecedent: Optic flow stimuli (various 2D trajectories)
findings.mechanism: Integration of instantaneous perceptions of heading directions.
findings.quote: Our results indicate that it is possible to reconstruct travelled paths from optic flow.

findings.antecedent: Optic flow stimuli (translation and yaw unyoked)
findings.consequent: Illusory percepts (e.g., curvilinear movement perceived during linear translation with yaw)
findings.mechanism: Optic flow resembles that of another movement, and insufficient information to choose between alternatives, leading to perception of the simplest matching manoeuvre.
findings.quote: Stimuli in which translation and yaw are unyoked can give rise to illusory percepts

findings.antecedent: Simulated yaw (Ψo) relative to simulated translation (large amount)
findings.quote: When the stimulus simulated a relatively large amount of yaw relative to the simulated translation, subjects often reproduced a rotation in place.

findings.antecedent: Simulated observer orientation fixed in space (e.g., semicircle no-turn)
findings.quote: When the observer's orientation is fixed in space (conditions linear lateral or oblique and semicircle no-turn), performance is generally good.

findings.antecedent: Simulated observer orientation fixed only relative to trajectory OR not at all
findings.quote: Performance decreases when the orientation is fixed only relative to the trajectory, or not at all.

findings.antecedent: Simulated trajectory radius (larger)
findings.quote: Performance is generally better at the larger radius.

findings.antecedent: Simulated trajectory radius (small)
findings.quote: When the radius was small, there were instead many rotation-in-place responses.

findings.antecedent: Optic flow stimuli (complex manoeuvres)
findings.quote: Subjects appear to be capable to approximate the angle over which they are rotated, even during complex manoeuvres (figure 3).

findings.antecedent: Linear+yaw stimuli (smaller rotations)
findings.mechanism: Overshoot in perception.
findings.quote: A small range effect occurs for the linear+yaw stimuli: overshoot for the smaller rotations

findings.antecedent: Linear+yaw stimuli (large rotation, Ψo=360°)
findings.mechanism: Undershoot in perception.
findings.quote: and undershoot for the large rotation (Ψo=360°).

findings.antecedent: Stimulus does not simulate any observer rotation
findings.quote: Yaw is never perceived when the stimulus does not simulate any observer rotation

findings.antecedent: Simulated orientation fixed in environment (Ψo ≈ 0°) OR tangential to trajectory
findings.mechanism: Perception is close to veridical.
findings.quote: Perception is close to veridical when orientation remains approximately fixed in the environment (Ψo ≈ 0°), and when it is tangential to the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: Simulated yaw (Ψo) in direction opposite to path rotation (Ψp)
findings.mechanism: Subjects assume detected rotation results mostly from path rotation, leading to misperception (e.g., straight paths or paths curving in wrong direction).
findings.quote: They respond in a similar manner when the simulated yaw is in the direction opposite to the direction in which the trajectory rotates.

findings.antecedent: Simulated yaw (Ψo) > path rotation (Ψp) (e.g., linear+yaw conditions where Ψp=0°)
findings.mechanism: Subjects assume detected rotation results mostly from path rotation, leading to misperception.
findings.quote: When the orientation changes relative to the trajectory, such that Ψo>Ψp... subjects seem to assume that the detected rotation results (mostly) from a rotation of the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: Simulated manoeuvre: semicircle half-counter (clockwise semicircle with counterclockwise half-turn of observer)
findings.mechanism: Strong misattribution of yaw to path rotation, resulting in a perceived straight line.
findings.quote: in condition semicircle half-counter... the average perceived path is more or less a straight line.

findings.antecedent: Simulated manoeuvre: semicircle full-counter
findings.mechanism: Strong misattribution of yaw to path rotation, resulting in a perceived three-quarter counterclockwise arc.
findings.quote: In condition semicircle full-counter, the average response is a three-quarter counterclockwise arc!

findings.antecedent: Presence of a single landmark (linear+yaw conditions)
findings.mechanism: Landmark provides additional visual and/or extra-retinal information.
findings.quote: There are significant improvements in yaw and path perception for the linear+yaw conditions, when a landmark is present

findings.antecedent: Presence of a single landmark (linear+yaw conditions)
findings.mechanism: Landmark provides additional visual and/or extra-retinal information.
findings.quote: There are significant improvements in yaw and path perception for the linear+yaw conditions, when a landmark is present

findings.antecedent: Presence of a single landmark (short linear+yaw translations)
findings.mechanism: Landmark improves perception of the ego-motion component that is relatively weak (translation).
findings.quote: The improvement of the perception of the path is largest for the short translations

findings.antecedent: Presence of a single landmark (long linear+yaw translations)
findings.mechanism: Landmark improves perception of the ego-motion component that is relatively weak (rotation).
findings.quote: whereas the improvement in yaw is largest for the long translations.

findings.antecedent: Landmark type (shifting vs. fixated)
findings.consequent: Errors in yaw (Ψo) and path (Ψp) perception
findings.mechanism: Errors are smaller for a shifting landmark than for a fixated one.
findings.quote: The results suggest that the errors are smaller for a shifting landmark than for a fixated one.

findings.antecedent: Presence of a landmark (none vs. shifting vs. fixated)
findings.mechanism: Landmark provides additional visual and/or extra-retinal information. Effect mostly due to angular component, with fixated landmark having largest effect.
findings.quote: The benefit of a landmark is also apparent from the normalised figural distance (ANOVA none vs. shifting vs. fixated; F(2,30)=4.58, p<0.0184; mostly due to the angular component), but for this measure, the effect of the fixated landmark is the largest.

findings.antecedent: Presence of a landmark (none vs. shifting vs. fixated)
findings.mechanism: Landmark helps disambiguate ego-motion perception.
findings.quote: The number of erroneous RIP responses decrease when a landmark is present (ANOVA none vs. shifting vs. fixated; F(2,30)=4.81, p<0.0154).

findings.antecedent: Presence of a fixated landmark (semicircular conditions)
findings.mechanism: Landmark provides additional visual and/or extra-retinal information.
findings.quote: the angular figural distance (a measure of yaw perception) decreases in those conditions when a fixated landmark is present (ANOVA, F(1,14)=6.26; p<0.0254).

findings.antecedent: Simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally more yaw (short trajectory version)
findings.quote: the perception of path rotation benefited more from the presence of a landmark when the simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally more yaw (that is, more in the short trajectory version than in the long version).

findings.antecedent: Simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally less yaw (long trajectory version)
findings.quote: Perception of yaw improved more due to a landmark when the simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally less yaw (that is, more in the long version than in the short version).

findings.antecedent: Presence of a landmark (semicircle inward conditions)
findings.consequent: Exclusion of responses from analysis (due to erroneous perception)
findings.mechanism: Landmark served as a reference for movement of other points, reducing ambiguity.
findings.quote: Much less responses to the conditions semicircle inward were excluded from analysis when the stimulus contained a landmark that only served as a reference for the movement of the other points, compared to when there was no landmark.

findings.antecedent: Presence of a landmark
findings.mechanism: Landmark helps disambiguate ego-motion perception.
findings.quote: There were also less erroneous rotation in place responses when a landmark was present.

findings.antecedent: Presence of a landmark (majority of curvilinear conditions)
findings.mechanism: Additional information was either not useful or attention needed to interpret it interfered with ego-motion perception.
findings.quote: In the majority of these conditions, however, there was little effect of adding a landmark, and sometimes even a negative effect.

mechanisms: When yaw is unyoked to the path, detected rotation is mostly attributed to a rotation of the trajectory, leading to misperception.
Illusory percepts arise when optic flow resembles another movement, and insufficient information exists to choose between alternatives, leading to the perception of the simplest matching manoeuvre.
Landmarks provide additional visual and/or extra-retinal information (from eye-movements) that helps disambiguate ego-motion components (translation or rotation) depending on the manoeuvre type.
The structuring of an environment (additional elements beyond basic dots) needs to fulfill certain conditions to be useful, depending on the simulated manoeuvre.
moderators: Proportion of simulated yaw relative to path rotation
implementation_implications: Adding a single landmark can improve perception of ego-motion, particularly for linear+yaw conditions and specific curvilinear manoeuvres, suggesting its utility in virtual environments for navigation training or simulation.

tables.description: Lists stimulus conditions, descriptions, size (length/radius), experiments presented in, and landmark type (s=shifting, f=fixated).
Summary of results per condition: globally correct responses, trajectory correct responses, rotation in place responses, total responses (N), and quantitatively analysed responses (N*).

limitations: The task was perceived as difficult by subjects.
Subjects often reproduced a rotation in place when yaw was large relative to translation.

The good perception of yaw might partly be a result of an observational and/or response strategy, as stimuli simulated manoeuvres with multiples of 90° and 180° of rotation, and subjects seemed to categorize in steps of at least 90°.
The recorded reproductions did not always exactly match verbal descriptions, making it difficult to ascertain if the reproduction reflected actual perception or a categorisation/sloppy reproduction.
The study did not measure scale (radius) directly, making results not directly comparable to some other studies on curvature perception.
The HMDs used (VR4 and Datavisor LCD) had some cushion distortion in the corners of the view, which is a common problem with HMDs.

control_conditions: conditions with and without a single landmark

mechanism_chain.description: Optic flow stimuli and landmark information are processed by the visual system, integrated to form a perceived trajectory, which is then used for the reconstruction of travelled paths.

steps.from_construct: Optic flow stimuli and landmark information
steps.to_construct: Visual processing of motion and spatial cues
